intro: Question words (what, where, when, who, why, how…) make open questions: questions that ask for information. The secret is word order: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb.
objectifs: Know the question words and their meaning: what, where, when, who, why, how, which, whose.
Make questions in the right order with be, do / does, can and the present continuous.
Use How + adjective (how old, how often, how far) and What + noun (what time, what colour).
Put the preposition at the end of the question (Where are you from?).

texte: Most of them start with “wh-”, so we call them Wh- words; “how” is in the same family. The question word always comes at the start of the question.

lignes: How do you go to work?
a choice from a small group
Which bus goes to the centre?

sections.note: We usually answer “Why?” with “because”: “Why are you tired? — Because I work at night.”

sections.titre: Word order: Wh- + auxiliary + subject + verb
texte: In English, you can't keep the order of a statement in a question (“Where you live?” is wrong). You need an auxiliary before the subject.
With “be”, “can” or the present continuous, the auxiliary is already there: just put it before the subject. With the present simple, add “do” or “does”; the main verb is then in the base form (no s).
Remember QASI: Question word, Auxiliary, Subject, Infinitive (base verb).
exemples: Where does your sister work? — In a bank.
What are you reading? — A novel.

texte: “How” goes with an adjective or adverb to ask about a measure: how old (age), how tall (height), how far (distance), how long (time), how often (frequency). “How much / how many” are in lesson 30.
“What” and “which” go with a noun: what time, what colour, what kind of music. Use “which” when the choice is small and known (Which one, the red or the blue?) and “what” when the choice is open.
“Whose” + noun asks about the owner: “Whose car is this? — It's Marc's.” Don't confuse it with “Who's” (= who is), which sounds the same.
exemples: How old is your daughter? — She's six.
How often do you go to the gym? — Twice a week.
How far is the airport? — About ten kilometres.
What kind of music do you like?
Which colour do you want, blue or green?

texte: When a verb has a preposition (be from, talk to, look at, wait for), the preposition stays at the end of the question in normal English: “Where are you from?”, not “From where are you?”.
This is the normal form in speaking and in writing.
exemples: Where are you from? — I'm from Cameroon.

texte: When “who” or “what” is the subject of the verb (you ask WHO does the action), don't use “do / does”: “Who lives here?”. Compare: “Who do you love?” (“you” is the subject).
At this level, learn the common questions: “Who wants coffee?”, “What happens next?”. Lesson 68 looks at this in more detail.

formule: Question word + auxiliary (is / are / do / does / can) + subject + verb…? — Where do you live?
prononciation: In what, where, when, why, which, “wh” sounds like /w/: /wɒt/, /weə/, /wen/, /waɪ/. But who, whose and whom start with /h/: /huː/, /huːz/.
In a Wh- question, the voice goes down at the end (like a statement): “Where do you LIVE? ↘”.
In fast speech, “do you” gets short: “Where do you live?” ≈ /ˈweə dʒə ˈlɪv/; “What do you” ≈ /ˈwɒdʒə/.
Common short forms: what's /wɒts/, where's /weəz/, who's /huːz/, how's /haʊz/.
“Whose” and “who's” sound exactly the same: /huːz/. The context shows the difference.
erreurs: You need the auxiliary “do” before the subject.
After “does”, use the base verb, no s.
Ask about age with “How old + be”.
The preposition stays at the end.
What's your brother called? / What's your brother's name?
Ask about names with What's … called? / What's … name?
With “be”, put the verb before the subject.
When “who” is the subject, no “do / does”.

dialogue.contexte: At a conversation café in Montreal, Julie meets Emmanuel, who is new from Cameroon.
lignes: I'm Emmanuel. Nice to meet you.
Cool! Why are you in Montreal?
Because I'm a student at the university. I study engineering.
And how often do you come to this café?
Every Thursday. What about you? What do you do?
“What do you do?” = What's your job?
I'm a nurse. Which language do you want to practise tonight, English or French?

exercices.consigne: Complete with what, where, when, who, why, how or whose.
items: ___ is that woman? — She's my aunt.
___ are you sad? — Because my cat is ill.
___ do you go to work? — By bus.

exercices.consigne: Put the words in the right order to make a question.
items: does / what time / start / the film
What time does the film start?

exercices.consigne: Write the question for the part in CAPITAL LETTERS.
items: What time does the film start?
I go to the gym TWICE A WEEK.
How often do you go to the gym?

exercices.consigne: Each question has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: What's your sister's name? / What's your sister called?

exercices.consigne: You meet a new colleague. Write five different questions with five different question words.
items: What's your name? Where are you from? Where do you live? How do you come to work? What do you do at the weekend?

a_retenir: Order: question word + auxiliary + subject + verb (QASI): Where do you live? What are you doing?
Present simple: do / does + base verb (Where does she work?).
How old / how often / how far / how long; What time / what colour / what kind of; which = small choice; whose = owner.
The preposition stays at the end: Where are you from? Who are you waiting for?
The voice goes down at the end of a Wh- question.
